# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The expansion of transcatheter therapies for structural heart disease has created an urgent need for large-bore vascular access in patients with prohibitive iliofemoral, aortic, or other peripheral arterial anatomy [1,2]. While transfemoral access remains the preferred route for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), up to 15% of candidates have unsuitable peripheral arteries due to small caliber, calcification, or tortuosity [3]. Alternative access strategies—including transapical, transaortic, transaxillary/subclavian, and transcarotid routes—carry their own morbidity profiles [4,5]. Transcaval access, introduced as a percutaneous, fully endovascular alternative, exploits the proximity of the inferior vena cava (IVC) to the abdominal aorta to deliver large-bore devices [6,7].

## Technique and Rationale

Transcaval access involves crossing from the IVC into the abdominal aorta below the renal arteries, typically using an electrified guidewire to traverse the aortocaval space [6,8]. The technique was pioneed in preclinical models before translation to humans, demonstrating that the retroperitoneal space could tamponade bleeding owing to the higher aortic pressure decompressing into the lower-pressure caval system [7,9]. After device delivery and procedure completion, the aortocaval tract is closed using a nitinol occluder device, most commonly a duct occluder [10,11].

Procedural planning relies heavily on contrast-enhanced computed tomography to identify a calcium-free aortic target and an adequate crossing window free of interposed structures such as bowel or major lumbar vessels [12,13]. The optimal crossing site is generally between the renal arteries and the aortic bifurcation [14].

## Clinical Evidence

The first-in-human and early feasibility experiences established that transcaval access could be achieved reliably with acceptable safety [6,15]. A prospective multicenter U.S. investigational device exemption study by Greenbaum and colleagues reported successful transcaval access in 99 of 100 patients undergoing TAVR or endovascular procedures, with successful closure in the majority [16]. Subsequent registries confirmed reproducibility across centers [17,18].

Comparative analyses suggest that transcaval TAVR outcomes are competitive with other alternative access routes [19,20]. Data from large registries indicate that transcaval access may be associated with lower mortality than transapical or transaortic approaches, in part by avoiding thoracotomy and general surgical exposure [21,22]. The transcaval approach has also been used to facilitate transcatheter mitral and tricuspid interventions, as well as delivery of mechanical circulatory support and other large-bore devices [23,24].

## Complications and Management

The principal concern with transcaval access is bleeding from the aortocaval tract [25]. Although the retroperitoneal pressure gradient often limits hemorrhage, clinically significant bleeding and the development of arteriovenous fistulae can occur [16,26]. Residual aortocaval fistula after closure is observed in a subset of patients, though many close spontaneously or remain hemodynamically inconsequential [27]. Other complications include retroperitoneal hematoma, the need for transfusion, and rarely the requirement for covered stent placement or surgical repair [28].

Refinements in technique—including meticulous CT-based site selection, use of dedicated crossing wires, and optimized closure strategies—have improved safety over time [12,29]. Operator experience and adherence to standardized protocols are key determinants of success [17]. Newer purpose-built closure devices are under investigation to further reduce residual fistula and bleeding rates [30].

## Future Directions

Transcaval access has matured from an experimental concept to an established alternative for patients lacking suitable transfemoral access [16,21]. As transcatheter therapies expand to younger patients and to mitral and tricuspid applications requiring ever-larger delivery systems, the demand for reliable non-femoral large-bore access will grow [23,24]. Priorities for future research include randomized or prospectively matched comparisons against transcaval and surgical alternatives, development of dedicated closure technologies, and refinement of imaging-based patient selection algorithms [29,30]. Standardized training pathways will be essential to disseminate the technique safely beyond high-volume expert centers [17,18].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access represents an elegant solution to the persistent challenge of large-bore vascular access in structural heart intervention. By leveraging the anatomic relationship of the IVC and aorta, it offers a fully percutaneous alternative that avoids surgical chest access. Accumulating evidence supports its safety and efficacy in carefully selected patients, though bleeding and residual fistula remain important considerations. With ongoing device innovation and growing operator experience, transcaval access is poised to play an increasing role in the contemporary structural heart toolkit.
